One campaign holds several ad sets, and each ad set holds several ads, so you can compare like with like.

A common beginner mistake is to make one campaign per ad. That spreads a small budget so thin that Meta never learns anything. A better habit is **one campaign per business goal**, a small number of ad sets (often one to three), and three to five ads inside each ad set so Meta can show more of the ones that work.
How the auction decides who sees your ad

Each time someone opens Facebook or Instagram, Meta holds an instant auction among all the ads that could be shown to that person. The winner is not simply the highest payer. Meta explains that it picks the ad with the highest **total value**, which combines three things:
**Bid**: how much the advertiser is willing to pay for the result. With the default Highest volume bid strategy, Meta sets this automatically from your budget.
**Estimated action rate**: Meta's prediction of how likely this person is to do what you asked for, such as click, send a message or buy.
**Ad quality**: signals from people's feedback, for example whether they hide the ad, and whether the ad uses low-quality tricks like engagement bait or withheld information.

This is why a good ad can beat a bigger budget. If your ad is relevant and people respond to it, your estimated action rate and quality rise, you win more auctions, and each result costs less. A dull or misleading ad pays more for every result even with the same targeting.
Read the relevance diagnostics

In the ad-level report you can add the columns Quality ranking, Engagement rate ranking and Conversion rate ranking. They compare your ad with ads competing for the same audience. They need enough impressions before they appear, so judge them only after the ad has run for a few days.
The learning phase

When an ad set starts, or after a significant edit, it enters the **learning phase**. Meta is exploring who responds. Results are often unstable and costs can be higher. Meta's guidance is that an ad set usually needs about **50 optimisation events within 7 days** (for example 50 purchases, or 50 leads) to exit learning. If it cannot get there, Ads Manager shows the status **Learning limited**.

Significant edits include changing the targeting, the creative, the optimisation event, or making a large budget change. Every one can send the ad set back into learning. So the professional rule is simple: **plan properly, launch, then leave it alone for several days** unless something is clearly broken, such as a wrong link or a policy rejection.
Worked example: restructuring a messy account

For example, Amaka sells ready-to-wear dresses through a Shopify-style website and Instagram. Her account has 9 active campaigns, each with one ad set, one ad and a budget of 2,000 naira a day (amounts approximate). She gets about 3 website sales a week in total.
Total daily spend is 9 × 2,000 = 18,000 naira, or 126,000 naira a week.
Each campaign gets about 3 ÷ 9 = 0.33 sales a week. None can come close to 50 events in 7 days, so all are stuck in learning.
She pauses all 9 and creates one Sales campaign optimising for Purchase, with one broad ad set (women 22 to 50, Nigeria's main cities she delivers to) at 18,000 naira a day.
Inside it she places her 5 best-performing creatives from the old campaigns, so Meta can compare them in one place.
Because purchases are still far fewer than 50 a week, she also notes that she may need to optimise for an earlier event such as Add to cart (Lesson 1.3 explains the trade-off).
The same 18,000 naira a day now feeds one ad set instead of nine, so all the purchase signals teach a single delivery system and she can see clearly which creative sells.

Conversion location and optimisation event

Inside each objective, the ad set asks **where** the result happens (the conversion location: website, app, Messenger, WhatsApp, Instagram, instant form or calls) and **which event** to optimise for. For a Nigerian business that closes sales on WhatsApp, a common set-up is Engagement or Sales with the conversion location set to WhatsApp, optimising for conversations. For a website shop, it is Sales with the website location and the Purchase event.

There is a tension here. The event closest to money (Purchase) is the best signal but the rarest. An earlier event (Add to cart, or Initiate checkout) happens more often, so the ad set learns faster, but some of those people never pay. A useful rule: optimise for the deepest event you can get **around 50 times a week** per ad set, and move deeper as volume grows.

The numbers you will judge every campaign by
**Reach**: number of different people who saw the ad. **Impressions**: total times it was shown.
**Frequency** = impressions ÷ reach. The average number of times each person saw it.
**CPM** (cost per mille) = spend ÷ impressions × 1,000. The price of being seen.
**CTR** (link click-through rate) = link clicks ÷ impressions × 100. How attention-grabbing the ad is.
**CPC** (cost per link click) = spend ÷ link clicks.
**Cost per result** = spend ÷ results, where the result is the event you optimised for.
**ROAS** (return on ad spend) = revenue from the ads ÷ spend.
Worked example: two ad sets, one honest verdict

For example, Funmi sells skincare from her website. She runs two ad sets for a week, each spending 35,000 naira (amounts approximate). Ad set A uses the Traffic objective. Ad set B uses Sales optimised for Purchase.
A: 70,000 impressions, 25,000 reach, 1,400 link clicks, 4 purchases worth 72,000 naira.
B: 35,000 impressions, 14,000 reach, 420 link clicks, 11 purchases worth 198,000 naira.

Ad set A looks better on every cheap metric (half the CPM, a third of the CPC) but B produced almost three times the revenue for the same spend. Judge campaigns on cost per result and ROAS, and use CPM, CTR and CPC only to diagnose why.
Diagnose with the cheap metrics

If cost per result is too high, look upstream. High CPM suggests a narrow or competitive audience. Low CTR suggests the creative is not stopping the scroll. Good CTR but few purchases suggests the problem is after the click: the landing page, price, delivery fee or trust.
Attribution: which purchases count

Meta credits a purchase to an ad only within an **attribution window**, set at ad set level. A commonly used default is **7-day click and 1-day view**: a purchase counts if it happened within 7 days of clicking the ad or within 1 day of seeing it. Add the Attribution setting column so you know which rule your numbers follow, and always compare Meta's reported sales with real orders in your shop or bank records. Meta reports what it can attribute, which is never perfectly the same as your till.

Advanced advertisers do the maths **before** they open Ads Manager. Without a target number, you cannot say whether an ad that gets sales at 4,000 naira each is excellent or ruinous. This lesson gives you three numbers to agree with every client: the **break-even cost per acquisition (CPA)**, the **target CPA**, and the **break-even ROAS**.
A person studying financial charts
The profit per order, not the size of the budget, tells you what you can afford to pay for a customer.
Step 1: profit per order before advertising

Start with the average order value (AOV), then subtract everything it costs to fulfil that order: the cost of the goods, packaging, payment processing fees (Paystack, Flutterwave and similar gateways charge a percentage per transaction; check the current rate on their pricing page), any delivery cost the business absorbs, and an allowance for returns. What is left is the **gross profit per order**. That is the most you could spend on ads to get one order and still break even.
Step 2: target CPA and break-even ROAS
**Break-even CPA** = gross profit per order.
**Target CPA** = a lower number that leaves the business real profit, for example 50 to 70 percent of break-even. Agree it with the owner.
**Gross margin** = gross profit per order ÷ AOV.
**Break-even ROAS** = 1 ÷ gross margin. Any ROAS below this loses money on the first order.
Worked example: a hair-care brand in Ibadan

For example, Kemi sells a hair growth oil set online. Her average order is 18,000 naira. Per order she pays (approximately) 6,500 naira for products, 800 for packaging, about 1.5 percent payment fee, and she subsidises delivery by 1,500 naira.
Payment fee: 18,000 × 0.015 = 270 naira.
Total cost per order: 6,500 + 800 + 270 + 1,500 = 9,070 naira.
Gross profit per order: 18,000 − 9,070 = 8,930 naira. This is her break-even CPA.
Gross margin: 8,930 ÷ 18,000 = 0.496, about 49.6 percent.
Break-even ROAS: 1 ÷ 0.496 = 2.02. Below about 2.0 she loses money on each first order.
She chooses a target CPA of 60 percent of break-even: 8,930 × 0.6 = 5,358, rounded to 5,400 naira, which is a target ROAS of 18,000 ÷ 5,400 = 3.33.
Kemi now judges every ad set against clear lines: below ROAS 2.0 pause or fix, between 2.0 and 3.3 improve, above 3.3 consider scaling.

Step 3: a budget that can learn

Now link the target to the learning phase. If an ad set needs about 50 optimisation events a week, and you expect each event to cost roughly your target CPA, then the weekly budget to exit learning is about **50 × expected cost per event**. For Kemi optimising for Purchase, that is 50 × 5,400 = 270,000 naira a week, about 38,600 naira a day. She has 15,000 naira a day.

When the budget is too small for the deepest event, you have three honest options. First, optimise for an earlier event: if Add to cart costs roughly 1,200 naira, 50 a week is 60,000 naira, within reach. Second, consolidate: one ad set instead of three. Third, accept Learning limited, run longer and judge on two to four weeks of data instead of one. What you must not do is promise a client a stable cost per sale from a budget that cannot produce the data.
Lifetime value is not an excuse

Some clients will say repeat customers justify a CPA above break-even. That can be true, but only with evidence: real repeat purchase records over several months. Without them, plan on first-order profit. Never let a client borrow money for ad spend on the strength of a hoped-for ROAS.
Nigerian realities that change the maths

**Payment on delivery**: if some orders are refused at the door, divide real profit by delivered orders, not placed orders. A 20 percent refusal rate means each ad-driven order is worth only 80 percent of what Meta reports, plus the wasted delivery cost.
**WhatsApp sales**: Meta cannot see a sale closed in a chat. Track conversations started (from Ads Manager) and orders closed (from your own record) to calculate a real cost per order.

**Paying Meta**: ad accounts can be billed in naira, but some bank cards have limits on online or international transactions. Confirm the payment method works before launch so ads do not stop mid-campaign. Check your Billing and payments page for any tax added to the charges.
**Exchange rates**: if the business imports stock, its costs move with the exchange rate. Recalculate break-even CPA whenever stock prices change.

Meta's business tools are organised in a **business portfolio** (previously called Business Manager), managed in **Business settings** and visible in Meta Business Suite. Conversions API: the server-side partner

Browser tracking misses some events: ad blockers, privacy settings, slow connections that close the page before the Pixel loads. The **Conversions API (CAPI)** sends the same events from the website's server directly to Meta. Meta recommends using it alongside the Pixel. Shopify and several WooCommerce plugins offer it through their Meta integration, so a non-developer can often switch it on. When both send the same event, each must carry the same **event ID** so Meta can remove the duplicate; check the deduplication status in Events Manager. Watch the **Event Match Quality** score there too: it rises when more customer information, such as email or phone, is passed in hashed form.

For example, Halima manages ads for a Kano bookshop's WooCommerce site. Ads Manager reports 40 purchases worth 1,120,000 naira in a week, but the shop's order list shows only 22 paid orders worth 610,000 naira (amounts approximate).
Reported ROAS on 200,000 naira of spend is 1,120,000 ÷ 200,000 = 5.6. Real ROAS from shop orders is 610,000 ÷ 200,000 = 3.05.
She opens the thank-you page with Pixel Helper and sees Purchase fire twice: once from a plugin and once from code a previous developer pasted into the theme.
In Events Manager, deduplication shows browser and server events arriving without a shared event ID.

She removes the pasted theme code, keeps the plugin, enables its Conversions API option, and places a test order: Purchase now fires once with an event ID, and the server event is marked as deduplicated.
Reporting now matches the shop within a small margin, so decisions are based on a true ROAS of about 3, not an inflated 5.6.

Use custom audiences in two ways. First, **retargeting**: show a reminder or offer to people who added to cart in the last 14 days but did not buy (create the audience as AddToCart in 14 days, then exclude Purchase in 14 days). Second, **exclusion**: stop paying to show 'first order' ads to existing customers by excluding your customer list or purchasers.
Lookalike audiences

A **lookalike** asks Meta to find new people who resemble a source audience. You choose a country and a size from 1 to 10 percent of that country's users: 1 percent is closest to the source, 10 percent is broadest. Meta needs at least 100 people from one country in the source, and better sources give better lookalikes. A list of your 600 best repeat customers usually beats a list of 5,000 people who once liked a post.
Broad and Advantage+ audience

With **Advantage+ audience**, your age and interest choices become suggestions and Meta may go beyond them if it predicts better results. Broad targeting (just location, and age where legally needed) works best when the Pixel has a healthy history of purchase events. For a brand-new account with no data, sensible suggestions plus a strong lookalike can help Meta start faster. Location, though, stays a hard rule: if the business delivers only in Lagos, set Lagos.
Testing that actually answers a question

Ads Manager has an **A/B test** tool (from the Experiments area, or from the toolbar on a campaign or ad set). It splits people randomly so the same person does not see both versions, then reports a winner and how confident Meta is that the result would repeat. Four rules make a test worth running:
**One variable only**: creative, or audience, or placement, or the offer. Change two things and you cannot say which one mattered.
**A written hypothesis**: 'A customer-testimonial video will lower cost per purchase compared with a product-only video, because new buyers need trust.'

**Enough budget for a result**: each version should be able to reach a meaningful number of optimisation events. Ads Manager estimates test power when you set it up; if it warns the test is unlikely to find a winner, raise the budget, lengthen the time or test an earlier event.
**Fixed duration**: decide the length in advance (often 7 to 14 days) and do not stop early because one side is ahead on day two.

Worked example: is the budget big enough for a test?

For example, Ruth runs ads for a solar lamp distributor in Port Harcourt that sells on its website. Recent cost per purchase is about 4,000 naira (approximate). She wants to test a demonstration video against a price-led carousel, aiming for at least 30 purchases per version so the result means something.
Purchases needed: 30 per version × 2 versions = 60.
Expected spend: 60 × 4,000 = 240,000 naira.
Over 14 days, that is 240,000 ÷ 14 = about 17,100 naira a day, split between the two versions.
The client's test budget is only 8,000 naira a day, which would buy about 8,000 × 14 ÷ 4,000 = 28 purchases in total, only 14 per version.
Ruth changes the test event to AddToCart, which costs about 900 naira: 112,000 naira over 14 days buys about 124 add-to-carts, roughly 62 per version.
Instead of a purchase test too small to trust, she runs an add-to-cart test with about 60 events per side, then confirms the winner on purchases over the following weeks.

Record every test in a simple sheet: date, hypothesis, variable, budget, result, confidence, decision. After three months this log is worth more than any single campaign, because it tells you what this particular market responds to.
Custom audiences are for retargeting and for excluding existing buyers.
Lookalikes need at least 100 people from one country; quality of source matters most.
Broad and Advantage+ audience work best once the Pixel has purchase history.

Ad policies, launch QA, monitoring and documentation
Identify ad content and categories that Meta restricts
Run a pre-launch quality check on every campaign
Follow a monitoring rhythm for the first two weeks and recognise creative fatigue

Clients judge you on two things: results, and whether anything embarrassing or expensive happened. A rejected ad on launch day, a campaign that spent the month's budget overnight, or a report nobody understands will lose a client even when the numbers are good. This lesson is your professional safety system.
A person ticking items on a large checklist
A written pre-launch check catches the small errors that cause the biggest problems.
Policies that catch African advertisers out

All ads are reviewed against Meta's **Advertising Standards** (published on the Meta Transparency Center). Read the sections relevant to each client. Common causes of rejection for small businesses include:
**Personal attributes**: copy that implies you know something personal about the viewer, such as 'Struggling with your weight?' or 'Are you in debt?'. Rewrite as 'Our programme helps people who...'.

**Health and beauty claims**: before-and-after images and promises of guaranteed results for weight loss or skin lightening. Herbal and supplement products also need any NAFDAC registration a product requires, and claims must be honest.
**Financial products and get-rich offers**: loans, investments, crypto and 'double your money' messages face extra rules, and some need prior written permission from Meta.
**Misleading features**: fake play buttons, fake notification dots, or headlines that hide what the ad is about.

**Special Ad Categories**: ads about housing, employment, credit or financial services, and social issues, elections or politics must be declared, which limits some targeting options in many countries. Political and social issue ads also need authorisation and a 'Paid for by' disclaimer.
Disapproved is not the end

If an ad is rejected and you believe it complies, request a review from Account Quality. If it is a real breach, fix it rather than trying again with small wording changes. Repeated violations can restrict the whole ad account, which hurts the client far more than one lost ad.

Objective, conversion location and optimisation event match the plan.
Location, age and language are correct; exclusions (existing customers) are applied.
Budget, schedule and spending limit are right: check daily versus lifetime budget and the end date.
Every link opens on a phone, loads quickly on mobile data and lands on the right product.
Copy is checked for spelling, prices, phone numbers and delivery promises; prices match the website.
The ad preview looks right in Feed, Stories and Reels placements; text is not cut off.
The Pixel is selected in the ad's tracking section and the event shows as active in Events Manager.
Monitoring the first two weeks
Monitoring rhythm after launch
Hour 2: delivery started?
Day 1: spend and errors
Days 2 to 7: hands off
Day 7: first review
Day 14: decisions
Check often early for technical faults, but make performance decisions only when there is enough data.

In the first hours you are checking only for faults: is it delivering, is spend on track, are any ads rejected. During the learning phase, avoid optimisation edits. From day 7, compare each ad set with the target CPA from Lesson 1.3. Watch for **creative fatigue**: frequency climbing while CTR falls and cost per result rises. The fix is new creative, not a narrower audience. Meta's **automated rules** can help protect budget, for example pausing an ad set if it spends twice the target CPA without a result.
Naming, change log and reporting
Worked example: a naming convention and weekly report
For example, Chioma manages ads for a Lagos catering company. She uses a fixed naming pattern so anyone can read the account, and sends a Monday report (amounts approximate).
Campaign: 2026-10_Sales_WebPurchase_Catering. Ad set: LAG_Broad_25-55_AdvPlacements. Ad: VID_Testimonial_Hook1_v2.
Change log entry: '14 Oct, raised ad set budget from 15,000 to 18,000 naira/day (20%), reason: CPA 3,900 vs target 5,000 for 7 days.'
Report numbers: spend 126,000 naira, 31 purchases, revenue 527,000 naira.
Cost per purchase = 126,000 ÷ 31 = 4,065 naira. ROAS = 527,000 ÷ 126,000 = 4.18, against a break-even ROAS of 2.2.
Report text: what happened, why she thinks it happened, what she will change this week, and what she needs from the client (new photos of the jollof platter).
The client sees results in their own terms, every change has a reason and a date, and another manager could take over the account without guessing.

Write the weekly report for a busy business owner, not for another advertiser. Lead with the numbers they care about (orders, revenue, cost per order against target), then one short paragraph of explanation. Put CPM, CTR and frequency lower down for anyone who wants detail. Use the same layout every week so trends are easy to see.
Scale gently

When an ad set is beating target, increase its budget in modest steps (many practitioners use about 20 percent every few days) rather than doubling it, to avoid a large shake-up in delivery. Record each change in the log.

Winning and Running Client Accounts

Here you turn technical skill into paid work. You will run a discovery call and audit an existing ad account, price your management fairly and write a proposal that controls scope, then build a case-study portfolio and a 90-day plan to land and keep your first client.
Discovery calls and auditing an existing ad account
Run a discovery call that collects the numbers a campaign needs
Request account access safely through partner access
Audit an ad account for tracking, structure, creative and policy problems
Prioritise audit findings by impact and effort

Clients rarely arrive with a clean brief. They say 'my ads are not working' or 'I want more sales'. Your job in discovery is to turn that into numbers you can manage: what a customer is worth, what a sale costs today, what the budget really is, and what is broken in the current set-up. Done well, discovery also shows the client that you think like a business partner, not a button-pusher.
Two people on a video call taking notes
A structured discovery call turns a vague complaint into numbers you can manage.
The discovery call: five groups of questions
Area
Questions to ask
Business economics
What is your average order value? What does each order cost you to fulfil? How many customers buy again, and how soon?
Sales process
Where do sales close: website, WhatsApp, phone, shop? Who answers messages, and how fast? What share of delivery orders are refused?
Customers
Who are your best customers? Where do they live? Why do they choose you over competitors? What objections do they raise?
History and assets
What have you tried in ads? What worked? Do you have a customer list collected with consent, product photos, videos, reviews?
Constraints
What monthly ad budget can you sustain for at least three months? Any products or claims that need NAFDAC, CAC or other approval? Busy seasons and stock limits?
Listen for the real bottleneck

If a client says they get many WhatsApp messages but few orders, more ads will not help. The problem may be slow replies, unclear prices or delivery fees. Say so. Honest diagnosis wins more long-term clients than taking money for ads that cannot work.
Getting access safely

Ask the client to add your business portfolio as a **partner** on their ad account, Page, Instagram account and dataset (Pixel), with the access level you need. Never accept a password, and never offer to 'create a new account for them' that you control. If the client has no business portfolio, walk them through creating one themselves on a video call. Before auditing, ask for read-only access if they are not yet paying you.
The account audit
Look at the last 90 days and work through four areas. Write down evidence for each finding (a screenshot or a number), because the audit becomes your sales document.
**Tracking**: Is there a Pixel? Which events fire? Does Purchase send value and currency? Does Meta's purchase count roughly match real orders? Is the domain verified? Is the Conversions API on?
**Structure**: How many active campaigns and ad sets? Are they Learning limited? Are budgets spread too thin? Are existing customers excluded from prospecting?
**Creative**: How many ads are active? How old are they? What are frequency, CTR and the relevance rankings? Is there video made for vertical placements?
**Account health**: Any rejected ads or restrictions in Account Quality? Who has access, and do they all still need it? Is two-factor authentication on?

Quick wins: do first
Big projects: plan next
Small fixes: batch together
Low value: leave for later
Effort (low to high)
Impact (high at top)
Sort every finding by impact and effort, then present quick wins first so the client sees progress in week one.
Worked example: an audit for an Abuja interior décor shop

For example, Grace is asked to review the ads of an Abuja décor shop that spent about 300,000 naira last month with 'no results'. The shop sells through its website and Instagram DMs. Average order is 45,000 naira and the owner says gross profit per order is about 18,000 naira.
Break-even CPA is 18,000 naira; break-even ROAS is 1 ÷ (18,000 ÷ 45,000) = 1 ÷ 0.4 = 2.5.
Tracking: the Pixel fires PageView only. There is no Purchase event, so all 6 campaigns use the Traffic objective. Meta has never been told what a sale looks like.
Structure: 6 campaigns × 50,000 naira = 300,000 naira; 4,200 link clicks at about 71 naira each, and the shop recorded 5 website orders (225,000 naira revenue), a real ROAS of 0.75.
Creative: three ads, all over four months old, frequency above 6 in the retargeting campaign.
Prioritised: quick wins are installing Purchase with value, excluding past buyers and pausing the old retargeting ads; the big project is a new Sales campaign with fresh vertical video.
Grace presents a short audit with screenshots, shows that the shop paid about 60,000 naira per order against a break-even of 18,000, and proposes a fixed-price set-up followed by monthly management.
Present the audit, then stop talking

Share the audit on a call rather than only by email. Walk through the three quick wins, the cost per order today versus break-even, and what you would do in the first 30 days. Then ask the client what they think. Many owners have never seen their numbers laid out this way, and the conversation that follows is often where they decide to hire you.

Pricing management, writing the proposal and controlling scope
Compare flat-fee, percentage-of-spend and hybrid pricing models
Calculate a management fee from your time and costs
Write a proposal with deliverables, limits and reporting cadence
Handle requests that fall outside the agreed scope

There are always two separate amounts in paid advertising work. **Ad spend** goes to Meta, ideally charged directly to the client's own payment method inside their ad account. Your **management fee** pays for your expertise and time. Keeping these separate protects you: you are never out of pocket if Meta charges more than expected, and the client can see every naira of spend in their own billing history.
Two people shaking hands over a deal
A clear proposal and agreed scope make the handshake the start of a good working relationship.
Three pricing models
Flat fee versus percentage of spend
Flat monthly fee
Percentage of ad spend
Predictable for both sides
Rewards efficiency, not bigger spend
Must be revised as work grows
Grows as the account scales
Can tempt spending more than needed
Unfair to you at small budgets
Many freelancers use a hybrid: a flat minimum fee plus a percentage above an agreed spend level.

There is no official price list for this work. Rates depend on your experience, results and the client's size. Instead of guessing, build your fee from your time, then check it against what local businesses can afford and what comparable freelancers charge on platforms such as Upwork or in your network.
Worked example: pricing a first retainer

For example, Bisi is newly certified and wants to manage a Lagos fitness studio's ads (amounts approximate and illustrative, not market rates). The client will spend 400,000 naira a month on ads. Bisi wants to earn about 7,500 naira per working hour.
Monthly time: 2 hours a week on optimisation and creative briefs (8 hours), a weekly report at 1 hour each (4 hours), a monthly call and planning (2 hours). Total 14 hours.
Base fee: 14 × 7,500 = 105,000 naira. She adds 10 percent for tools and data: 105,000 × 1.10 = 115,500, rounded to 115,000 naira.
Check against percentage pricing: 115,000 ÷ 400,000 = 28.75 percent of spend, which will feel very high to the client.
She reduces her time by using one shared dashboard and fortnightly instead of weekly calls, to 11 hours: 11 × 7,500 × 1.10 = 90,750, offered as 90,000 naira, about 22.5 percent of spend.
She adds a one-off set-up fee of 120,000 naira for the Pixel, Conversions API, audiences and the first creative batch, which takes about 16 hours.
Bisi offers 120,000 naira set-up plus 90,000 naira a month for three months, then a review. If spend rises above 600,000 naira a month, the fee becomes 90,000 plus 10 percent of spend above 600,000.
What the proposal must say
**Goal and target**: the business goal and the agreed target CPA or ROAS, with the unit economics behind it.
**Deliverables**: number of campaigns, ad variations per month, tests per month, report frequency and calls.
**What the client provides**: product photos or video, fast replies to ad leads, approvals within an agreed time, payment method in the ad account.
**What is not included**: website building, photography, content for organic posts, replying to customer messages, unless priced separately.
**Honest expectations**: the first two to four weeks are for learning and testing; a small budget gives limited data; results are not guaranteed.
**Terms**: fee, payment dates (for example in advance each month by bank transfer or a Paystack payment link), notice period, and who owns the account, audiences and creative (the client).
Never guarantee results

Promising 'triple sales in 30 days' is the fastest way to lose trust. Meta's auction, the client's prices, stock and customer service all affect results. Promise a process, a testing plan and transparent reporting instead.
Controlling scope

Scope creep is small requests that add up: 'just design our flyer', 'can you also post on our page', 'please reply to these comments'. Answer kindly and clearly: 'That is outside our agreement. I can do it for X, or I can recommend someone.' Keep a running list and raise it at the monthly review. If extra work becomes regular, update the proposal.

Put the agreement in writing, even if it is a short document both sides sign or approve by email. Take the management fee **in advance** each month, so you are never chasing payment for work already done. Agree a notice period, for example 30 days, so neither side is surprised. When a client leaves, hand over cleanly: remove your partner access only after giving them your change log, the final report and the naming convention, so their next manager can continue. A professional exit is often how you get a referral, or the client back later.

Clients buy evidence. A certificate shows you studied; a case study shows you can get results; a clear plan shows you will turn up. This lesson helps you build all three, even if you have never had a paying client.
A person presenting a portfolio website
A simple online portfolio with one or two strong case studies is your most persuasive sales tool.
Getting your first evidence
**Your own test**: run a small campaign for your own offer (a printable planner, a class, a product you resell) with a fixed budget, and document it fully.
**A supervised pilot**: offer a local business a short pilot at a reduced fee, with written permission to share anonymised results.
**An audit sample**: an audit (with permission) showing your thinking is also evidence, even before results.
The one-page case study
Worked example: turning a pilot into a case study

For example, Zainab ran a 4-week pilot for a Kaduna tailoring school selling a weekend course (amounts approximate). Before the pilot, the school's boosted posts produced enquiries but nobody tracked enrolments.
Situation: Lead objective with an instant form (Higher intent form type), conversion location Instant forms, 60,000 naira a week for 4 weeks = 240,000 naira.
Result in Ads Manager: 96 leads, so cost per lead = 240,000 ÷ 96 = 2,500 naira.
Result from the school's register: 18 enrolments at 35,000 naira = 630,000 naira. Lead-to-enrolment rate = 18 ÷ 96 = 18.75 percent.
Cost per enrolment = 240,000 ÷ 18 = 13,333 naira. Revenue per naira spent = 630,000 ÷ 240,000 = 2.63.
What she did: tested a classroom video against a finished-garment carousel; the video won on cost per lead, so it received the budget from week 2.

Her case study reads: 'Weekend course enrolments: 18 from 240,000 naira of ad spend, about 13,300 naira per enrolment, using lead ads and a creative test. Figures shared with the school's permission.'

Structure every case study the same way: **client and goal**, **starting point**, **what you did** (objective, audiences, tests), **results** in the client's terms with the period and spend, and **what you learned**. Use real numbers only, never round them up, and always state that you have permission or anonymise the client.
Credentials and research tools

**Meta Blueprint** (Meta's official training site) offers free self-paced courses on Ads Manager, measurement and creative, and paid professional certification exams for those who want a verifiable credential. Check the current exam list and fees on the site before you plan. The **Meta Ad Library** is free and public: search any brand to see all its currently active ads. Use it to research a prospect's competitors before a call, and to collect creative ideas for your niche.
Choose a niche

'I run Facebook ads' is hard to sell. 'I help Lagos and Abuja fashion brands that sell on Instagram get more website orders' is easy to remember and refer. A niche also makes your test log and case studies far more useful, because each lesson transfers to the next client.
Your 90-day plan

Each phase produces a piece of evidence that makes the next phase easier.

Days 16 to 30: run and document your own test campaign with a fixed budget you can afford to lose.

Outreach that gets replies

Keep the first message short, personal and useful. Mention something specific you saw in their ads or Instagram, offer one concrete observation, and ask a simple yes or no question. For example: 'Hello Tola, I saw your Ankara bag ads in the Ad Library. The video with the bag being packed is strong, but it links to your homepage, not the product. I help Lagos fashion brands get more website orders from Meta ads. Would a free 15-minute review of your ads be useful this week?' Send it to a named person, follow up once after a few days, and then stop. Track every message in a simple sheet so you learn which niches and messages respond.
Protect yourself from scams

New ad managers are targeted with fake 'job offers' that ask you to log in to Meta through a link or download 'campaign files'. Real clients add you as a partner from their own Business settings. Never run ads on an account you do not know, never pay to 'unlock' a job, and never run ads for products you suspect are fake or unregistered.

The auction
How Meta picks which ad to show
What you will pay for a result. With Highest volume, Meta sets it from your budget.
How likely this person is to click, message or buy.
Feedback such as hiding the ad, and low-quality tricks like engagement bait.
Each time someone opens Facebook or Instagram, Meta holds an instant auction. The winner is not simply the highest payer. It combines three things. First, your bid.
Second, how likely this person is to do what you asked.
Third, ad quality. So a relevant ad that people respond to wins more auctions, and each result costs less. A dull or misleading ad pays more.

Most failed campaigns are not killed by bad ads. They are killed by bad set-up: an ad account owned by someone who left, a Pixel that fires Purchase twice, or a card declined on day three.
This module builds the foundation properly, so the numbers you optimise on are real.
Before any ad runs
Set-up and safety checklist
The business owner should own the business portfolio, the ad account and the Pixel. You are added as a partner, never given their password, and if you leave they keep everything.
Turn on two-factor authentication for everyone, with two trusted admins. Test the payment method, verify the Pixel and the domain, and set an account spending limit as a safety net.
Check that your Pixel tells the truth
Purchase fires once, with the right value and NGN.
Open Test events in Events Manager
Browse, add to cart, start checkout
Check pages with Meta Pixel Helper
Place a real low-value test order
Add the Conversions API, same event ID
The Meta Pixel is a small piece of code that sends events, like add to cart or purchase, to Meta. Open Test events, then browse your site. Each event should appear within seconds.
Check each page with the free Meta Pixel Helper on a laptop. Then place a real low-value test order and refund it.
Add the Conversions API, which sends the same events from the server and recovers ones the browser misses. Both must carry the same event ID, so Meta removes duplicates.
Halima's shop showed 40 purchases in Ads Manager, but only 22 real paid orders. Purchase was firing twice. After the fix, ROAS fell from an inflated 5.6 to a true 3.05.
Audiences
Give Meta the right signals
Retarget: added to cart, did not buy
Exclude existing customers from first-order ads
Lookalike from your best repeat buyers
Go broad once the Pixel has purchase history
Custom audiences are people who already know you. Retarget people who added to cart in the last 14 days but did not buy.
And exclude existing customers, so you stop paying to show them first-order offers.

A lookalike asks Meta to find people who resemble a source. It needs at least 100 people from one country, and your 600 best repeat customers beat 5,000 people who once liked a post. Uploading a customer list needs their consent.
Broad targeting works best once your Pixel has purchase history. But location stays a hard rule. If you only deliver in Lagos, set Lagos.
